newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadians file lawsuit against insurers.
newsitem.headline: Canadians file lawsuit against insurers.

text.p: Canadian policy holders on Thursday launched a C$2 billion ($1.5 billion) lawsuit against two units of London Insurance Group Inc., and National Life Assurance Co. of Canada.

Lawyers representing policy holders told Reuters the suit was filed on behalf of thousands of Canadians who bought "vanishing premium" life insurance policies on the premise that the policy would retain its full value over the life of the holder after a fixed number of payments.
The lawsuit, which seeks class action status, alleges that the insurance companies in sales pitches to prospective customers misrepresented the payments needed to keep the policies in force.
London Insurance said it was unaware of the lawsuit.

"I have no knowledge of that whatsoever," Craig Postons, a spokesman for London Insurance, told Reuters. "Until we've read through what the claim is and what the situation is I don't think we'd have any further comment."
London Insurance is to be acquired by Royal Bank of Canada in a C$2.4 billion ($1.7 billion) deal announced last week.
A National Assurance spokesman could not be reached for comment.

The lawsuit alleges the policies were sold with vaguely worded contracts and that after the plaintiffs made the required number of payments, they were sent bills for more payments to keep their life insurance from lapsing.
"What they were saying in the presentation never got put into the contract," said John McLeish a partner in the Toronto-based law firm Loopstra, Nixon & McLeish, representing the policy holders.
McLeish said the suit, filed in the Ontario Court General Division, claims both general and punitive damages.
It alleges that starting in the early 1980s, the two companies began marketing whole-life policies that promised a limited number of premium payments -- after which the premiums would vanish.

The lawsuit alleges that customers were not told that the "vanishing" premiums were based on complex actuarial assumptions that were highly sensitive to interest rate movements. As interest rates fell, the premiums that were to have ended, continued.
One policy holder, Darryl Fish, told Reuters he was sold C$1 million ($728,000) of life insurance in 1989 by National Life Assurance based on five years of payments worth C$5,800 ($4,221) each year.
"After paying my five years of premiums I got another bill," he said.

The 38-year-old father of two said that when he questioned his insurance agent he was told that interest rates had fallen since he bought his policy and that it would lapse if he did not pay more money to keep it up.
"They were saying that it was based on interest rates and I said, 'Wait a second. No one ever said to me that it was based on any sort of interest rates,'" Fish said.
